questions.q: In retrosynthetic analysis, the Grignard reagent RMgBr serves as the synthetic equivalent of which synthon?
questions.e: A synthon is an idealized fragment; the reagent is its real-world equivalent.

questions.q: A β-hydroxy ketone (1,3-dioxygenated pattern) is most simply disconnected by a retro-:
questions.e: The Cα–Cβ bond is cut to give two carbonyl-derived fragments.

questions.q: A 1,5-dicarbonyl compound (or 5-oxo ester) is most commonly disconnected by a retro-:
questions.e: An enolate (donor) adds 1,4 to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (acceptor).

questions.q: Why do 1,4-dioxygenated and 1,2-dioxygenated patterns often require umpolung or unusual synthons?
c: The natural polarities of carbonyl chemistry (d¹ acceptors, d² donors) give 1,3 and 1,5 relationships, not 1,2 or 1,4
questions.e: Normal reactivity alternates acceptor/donor sites; 1,2 and 1,4 need a polarity reversal.

questions.q: Propose two retrosynthetic disconnections for triphenylmethanol.
questions.m: Disconnect one C–Ph bond: PhMgBr + benzophenone (Ph₂C=O) → Ph₃COH. Alternatively disconnect two C–Ph bonds: 2 PhMgBr + methyl (or ethyl) benzoate → Ph₃COH, since the ester adds two equivalents of Grignard.

questions.e: Deprotonation of the dithiane gives a nucleophilic acyl anion equivalent, unmasked by Hg²⁺ or NCS.

questions.q: Which of the following is a functional-group interconversion (FGI) used to enable a disconnection?
c: Converting an alcohol to a ketone by oxidation, to allow an enolate-based disconnection
questions.e: FGI changes the functional group without altering the skeleton.

questions.q: A tert-butyldimethylsilyl (TBS) ether is typically removed with:
questions.e: Si–F bonds are very strong, driving cleavage.

questions.q: Boc, Fmoc and Cbz amine protecting groups are respectively removed by:
questions.e: Their mutually different cleavage conditions make them orthogonal.

c: Nucleophiles and bases; removed with aqueous acid
questions.e: They are stable to bases, hydrides and organometallics.

questions.q: What is an orthogonal protecting-group strategy? Give an example.
questions.m: Protecting groups are orthogonal when each can be removed selectively in the presence of the others using mutually compatible conditions. Example: a molecule with a TBS ether (fluoride-labile), a benzyl ether (hydrogenolysis) and an acetate ester (base hydrolysis) — each can be unmasked independently in any order.

questions.e: Michael addition then intramolecular aldol condensation.

questions.q: According to Baldwin's rules, which ring closure is favored?
Ring-closing metathesis typically uses ____ and releases ____.
questions.e: Terminal alkenes close with loss of volatile ethylene.

questions.q: Distinguish chemoselectivity, regioselectivity and stereoselectivity with a brief example of each.
questions.m: Chemoselectivity: preference among functional groups (NaBH₄ reduces a ketone in the presence of an ester). Regioselectivity: preference among positions (hydroboration puts boron on the less substituted alkene carbon). Stereoselectivity: preference for one stereoisomer (Evans aldol giving syn product of defined absolute configuration).

questions.q: DIBAL-H at −78 °C converts an ester into:
questions.e: At low temperature the stable tetrahedral intermediate holds until workup, preventing over-reduction.

questions.q: NaBH₄ in ethanol will reduce which of these in a molecule containing all three?
c: The ketone, leaving the ester and amide
The ester and ketone, leaving the amide
questions.e: NaBH₄ is a mild reductant; LiAlH₄ would reduce all three.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl chloride, with pyridine controlling stereochemical course in chiral 2° cases?
questions.e: Thionyl chloride gives alkyl chlorides; pyridine promotes clean SN2 inversion for secondary alcohols.
